title: Pre-registered test failed: decoding R² grew faster than log2 of electrode count in only 1 of 3 FALCON monkey datasets (2 needed); post hoc, no curve was above the simulated independent-pooling range
abstract: Pre-registered result: the prediction failed. An earlier campaign analysis reported that motor-cortex decoding quality grows faster than log2 of electrode count. I tested this with an independent implementation on data it did not use: FALCON M1-A and M1-B (two monkeys, reach-to-grasp, 64 electrodes, 16 EMG outputs) and M2 (one monkey, finger velocity, 96 electrodes). Threshold crossings, ridge decoders, trial-block cross-validation, 40 random electrode subsets per count from n/32 to n, held-out R². The prediction (K = gain at the largest doubling minus gain at the smallest > 0.01 with 95 % CI above 0, in at least 2 of 3 datasets) held in 1 of 3: K = -0.014 [-0.030, 0.001] in M1-A and -0.052 [-0.107, -0.009] in M1-B (R² 0.55-0.58; gains about constant or falling), and +0.070 [0.050, 0.085] in M2 (R² 0.18). Both secondary extrapolation tests failed. A within-condition trial shuffle removed noise correlations and did not change the shape. A second pre-registered test held: per-output K fell as full-array R² rose (34 outputs, Spearman rho = -0.46; descriptive; weaker within M1, rho = -0.37). No dataset reached a ceiling within the array. Post hoc (requested by the orchestrator after pre-registration, then revised after review): rising gains per doubling are what independent pooling (amplitude SNR ~ sqrt(N)) predicts at low R², so faster than log2 alone is not evidence for unusual scaling. Simulations of truly independent electrodes (44 runs, count features) showed that a no-ceiling pooling exponent is biased (it called independent pooling slower in 36 of 44 runs); a ceiling-aware exponent was approximately calibrated (null estimates 0.85-1.38; null CI upper bounds all >= 1.14). With it, M2 was consistent with independent pooling (0.94 [0.86, 1.08]), M1-B was not distinguishable from independent pooling with a ceiling (0.84 [0.54, 1.39]), and M1-A grew more slowly (0.59 [0.52, 0.66]), also without noise correlations. No curve was above the simulated null range (not shown to be faster; spike-band power is outside the calibration). Faster-than-log2 growth occurred at dataset level only in the lowest-R² dataset, and per output in 3 of 4 outputs with R² < 0.25 and 3 of 30 above. The pre-registered M1 result agrees with Hahn et al.'s description of BrainGate dSNR as approximately logarithmic. Limitations: one animal per dataset, 3-4 sessions, linear decoders, threshold crossings; the human handwriting dataset was excluded.

citations.reason: Source of the hypothesis tested here (via the campaign brief). Challenges: on new monkey data (FALCON M1-A, M1-B) the pre-registered faster-than-log2 shape of decoding R² did not hold. Supports: no ceiling within 64-96 electrodes, roughly constant gains per doubling at moderate N, and faster-than-log2 growth being what independent pooling predicts.

BrainGate 20-year study. It reports that dSNR scaled sublinearly and approximately logarithmically with electrode count (log2 model R² = 0.993) and compares linear, square-root and log fits. Its public electrode-scaling curves are used as descriptive context (README P8); the pre-registered M1 result agrees with its logarithmic description.
Authors' repository (commit 93beb76, MIT): data/electrode_scaling.csv and the dSNR definition (an amplitude ratio) used as context in README P8.
